questions.question: Investigate the panic button scenario using who, where, when and what, explain who else needs panic buttons and what existing solutions show, and list what the user herself would ask for.
questions.expected_answer: Who is Gogo Mahlangu, seventy-eight, living alone, slow-moving with arthritic hands, sleeping in one room, cooking in another and using an outside toilet; where is a small Mamelodi house with a yard, a neighbour across the fence most evenings, passing people in the street and no alarm company; when is a fall at night, a stranger at the door or in the yard, sudden illness or a paraffin stove fire; what help exists is the neighbour who would come if called, a daughter twenty minutes away with a phone, and passers-by who would notice a loud noise. Panic buttons also serve households worried about crime, elderly and disabled people alone, spaza owners, isolated farm workers, schools and domestic workers alone in large houses; commercial systems such as wireless buttons to armed response companies and location-sending apps show what works and what it costs, and their monthly fees of hundreds of rand exclude the households most at risk, so a loud local alarm from several points at an affordable price meets a real need. The user would ask for switches she can reach, buttons her weak hands can press, operation in the dark and during power cuts, buttons by the bed, stove and toilet, a way to silence a false alarm, and no monthly fee, each of which becomes a specification.

questions.question: Explain what a design brief is and its three parts, give a suitable brief for the scenario, and explain what a brief must and must not include.
questions.expected_answer: A design brief is a short statement written before any drawing that fixes what success means, in three parts: the problem, stating the need without naming a solution; the users, saying who will use it and what they are like; and the purpose, saying what the device must achieve. For the scenario: the problem is that an elderly woman living alone in Mamelodi has no reliable way to call for help from the rooms she uses, especially at night or when her phone is flat; the users are Gogo Mahlangu, slow-moving with weak hands and poor night vision, and the neighbour and passers-by who must hear and respond; the purpose is to design and make a battery-powered alarm system with a button at the bed, the stove and the outside toilet, any one of which sets off a loud siren and a bright light the neighbour can hear and see, and which Gogo can switch off herself. The brief must name the need, the user, the goal and facts of the need such as where buttons are required, and must not specify the type of switch, voltage or connection, which are design decisions; a brief that reads as a circuit description is a solution in disguise, one that is too vague could not be failed, and a good brief lets two designers produce two different designs that both satisfy it.

questions.question: Distinguish specifications from constraints, list the specifications for the panic button system, and list its constraints.
questions.expected_answer: Specifications are measurable, testable requirements the finished device must meet for the user; constraints are the limits of resources, time, materials and safety within which the design must work. Specifications: any one of three buttons at the bed, stove and toilet pressed alone must trigger the alarm; each button must be at least thirty millimetres across for the flat of a weak hand and mounted low enough to reach from the floor after a fall; the alarm must be audible across the fence, tested at the neighbour's door; a bright lamp visible from the street must also light for a hard-of-hearing neighbour and night passers-by; the system must run on batteries to work during load shedding and when prepaid is empty; buttons must glow or be marked for the dark; an indoor reset switch must let Gogo silence it; and standby must last at least a year on one set of batteries by drawing power only when triggered. Constraints: built from the class kit of cells, switches, buzzer, LEDs, resistors, wire and board; real component cost under a stated budget such as two hundred rand; low voltage only, never mains; buildable by the class in two sessions; toilet wiring weatherproof or wireless, shown in the model by a long lead; and documented with a circuit diagram and truth table.
